content: Cesarean sections (CS) are the most commonly performed major surgical procedure worldwide. Following a CS, a temporary reduction in bowel motility is expected. Although this condition typically resolves on its own within a few days, it can cause significant discomfort, necessitate the use of symptomatic medications, and delay hospital discharge, thereby increasing healthcare costs. Chewing gum during the immediate postoperative period has been proposed as a simple intervention that may facilitate the recovery of bowel function, as has been observed in other types of abdominal surgeries. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of chewing gum on reducing the duration of postoperative ileus and enhancing recovery after a CS. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, LILACS, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, as of June 20, 2016. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing chewing gum with standard care within the first 24 hours after a CS were included. Studies published solely in abstract form were also considered, but quasi-randomized, cross-over, or cluster-randomized trials were excluded. Two independent reviewers selected studies, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias using standard Cochrane methods. Dichotomous outcomes were reported as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), while continuous outcomes were presented as mean differences (MD) with 95% CI. A random-effects model was used to pool results in cases of significant heterogeneity, and the GRADE approach was employed to evaluate the overall quality of evidence. Seventeen RCTs involving 3,149 participants from nine countries were included in the review. Seven studies exclusively enrolled women undergoing elective CS (1,325 participants), while five studies focused on women having a primary CS (833 participants). Ten studies (1,731 participants) adhered to conventional feeding protocols, which involved withholding oral intake until the return of bowel function. The gum-chewing protocols varied across studies in terms of initiation time (immediately after CS to up to 12 hours later), session duration (15 to 60 minutes), and the number of sessions per day (three to more than six). Due to the nature of the intervention, blinding was not possible, and most outcomes were self-reported, leading to a high risk of bias across all studies. For the primary outcomes, women who chewed gum experienced a significantly shorter time to the passage of first flatus, with a mean reduction of seven hours compared to the control group (MD -7.09 hours, 95% CI -9.27 to -4.91 hours; 2,399 participants; 13 studies; very low-quality evidence). This effect was consistent across various subgroups, including primary and repeat CS, different gum-chewing regimens, and feeding protocols. Additionally, the incidence of ileus was reduced by over 60% in the gum-chewing group compared to controls (RR 0.39, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.80; 1,139 participants; four studies; low-quality evidence). Tolerance to gum-chewing was high, with only three women in one study reporting complaints, and no adverse effects were documented in eight studies involving 925 participants (low-quality evidence). For secondary outcomes, the time to the passage of feces was approximately nine hours earlier in the gum-chewing group (MD -9.22 hours, 95% CI -11.49 to -6.95 hours; 2,016 participants; 11 studies; very low-quality evidence). The duration of hospital stay was also shorter in the intervention group (MD -0.36 days, 95% CI -0.53 to -0.18 days; 1,489 participants; seven studies). Furthermore, the first intestinal sounds were detected earlier in the gum-chewing group (MD -4.56 hours, 95% CI -6.18 to -2.93 hours; 1,729 participants; nine studies). However, none of the studies assessed women's satisfaction with gum-chewing, and there was no significant difference in the need for analgesia or antiemetic agents between the intervention and control groups (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.12 to 2.13; 726 participants; three studies). The authors concluded that chewing gum in the immediate postoperative period after a CS is a well-tolerated intervention that appears to enhance the early recovery of bowel function. However, the overall quality of evidence was rated as very low to low due to high risks of bias, significant heterogeneity, and potential publication bias. Further research is needed to determine the optimal gum-chewing regimen, assess potential adverse effects, evaluate women's satisfaction, and ensure compliance with the intervention. Future studies should be large, well-designed, and methodologically rigorous to improve the quality of evidence and inform future updates of this review.
